about.text: PA Pharmacology Course · Lecture 2 · Session 1 of 2 — Musculoskeletal Pharmacology (Tuesday, October 27): pain, acetaminophen, NSAIDs, and osteoarthritis/rheumatoid arthritis pharmacotherapy, including DMARDs. The session follows one pathway — arachidonic acid — to see where each drug class steps in and how to treat musculoskeletal pain safely.
By the end you should be able to choose between acetaminophen, an NSAID, and a DMARD, and defend the choice.

definitions.text: **Nociceptive pain:** direct activation of pain receptors by tissue injury.
**Inflammatory pain:** pain driven by inflammatory mediators.
**Neuropathic pain:** pain from nerve injury or dysfunction.
**Acute pain:** recent onset, often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.
**Chronic pain:** persists beyond expected healing time, often > 3 months. Treatment approach differs sharply between acute and chronic pain.

how.text: **Tissue injury → release of inflammatory mediators → sensitization of nociceptors → pain.**
Key mediators: **prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).**
Arachidonic acid → COX enzyme → prostaglandins → pain and inflammation: the spine of the acetaminophen, NSAID, and corticosteroid sections.
**NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors act at the COX step; glucocorticoids act further upstream; cytokine inhibitors and analgesics act through separate, parallel pathways.**
**Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂** (membrane phospholipids → arachidonic acid), so a broad range of mediators falls. NSAIDs block only COX, so they lower prostaglandins specifically.
**Nociceptor sensitization:** injury releases PGE2, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines, which **lower the pain threshold** — normally harmless stimuli now hurt.
Prostaglandins sensitize nociceptors, so they are the main NSAID target; bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines are not blocked by NSAIDs.
Where drugs act: NSAIDs block COX; corticosteroids block PLA2 (phospholipase A₂) one step upstream.
**The immune response:** chronic inflammation involves eicosanoids, leukotrienes, cytokines, chemokines, and many immune cells; RA, SLE, vasculitis, and gout all stem from this cascade.
The lipoxygenase branch of arachidonic acid makes leukotrienes (chemotaxis, bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability) — a separate branch from the COX step NSAIDs block.

clinical.text: Most musculoskeletal pain in this lecture is a mix of nociceptive and inflammatory; pure neuropathic pain belongs to a separate pharmacology unit.
The mediator list is the roadmap for the lecture: NSAIDs target prostaglandins, biologic DMARDs target specific cytokines.

**Therapeutic strategies:** goal 1 is symptom relief and function (NSAIDs and DMARDs); goal 2 is slowing tissue damage, for which DMARDs are absolutely necessary. Response is tracked with indices such as DAS28 in RA.

examples.text: Corticosteroids (block phospholipase A₂) vs. NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors (block COX): two distinct points of intervention.

traps.text: Corticosteroids act **upstream** at phospholipase A₂, not at COX — that is why their effect is broader than an NSAID’s.
The lecture’s drugs target nociceptive and inflammatory pain; neuropathic pain is a different unit.

overview.text: Effective analgesia, with a narrow margin in overdose: treats pain and fever well, but is **not an anti-inflammatory drug** the way NSAIDs are.
Acetaminophen leaves inflammation alone; NSAIDs go after it directly.

moa.text: **Analgesic effect:** relieves mild-to-moderate pain, with a central mechanism that is still incompletely understood.
**Antipyretic effect:** reduces fever via central effects on the hypothalamic temperature-regulating center.
**Anti-inflammatory effect:** minimal at the periphery — unlike NSAIDs, acetaminophen is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent.
**Mechanism:** analgesia and antipyresis are mainly central, via reduced CNS prostaglandin synthesis; peripheral anti-inflammatory action is minimal.
Textbook adds: a weak peripheral COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor whose pain relief also involves opioid, cannabinoid, and serotonergic systems.

indications.text: Reasonable first-line for mild osteoarthritis pain.
Generally safer first-line than an NSAID in a patient with NSAID red flags (kidney disease, anticoagulation, older age).
Preferred over aspirin in aspirin allergy, hemophilia, peptic ulcer history, or aspirin-induced bronchospasm; alone it is inadequate for inflammatory conditions such as RA.

adverse.text: **Overdose: glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI accumulates, and hepatocyte injury follows.**
**Overdose cascade:** glucuronidation/sulfation saturate → more drug shunted to CYP2E1 → more NAPQI, glutathione exhausted → NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins → **centrilobular liver necrosis**.
Ingesting 15 g may be fatal (centrilobular hepatic necrosis); take care with liver disease, heavy alcohol use, or malnutrition.

contra.text: **Pearl:** chronic alcohol use and fasting lower GSH and raise risk; both also induce CYP2E1.

interactions.text: **Hidden overdose:** many combination cold, flu, and sleep products also contain acetaminophen — **unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen-related liver injury.**
Combining acetaminophen with an NSAID improves pain control but can potentiate the NSAID’s GI toxicity.

pk.text: Normal handling: acetaminophen → NAPQI (toxic metabolite) → glutathione conjugation → safe excretion.
NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine — the “toxic metabolite” example from Lecture 1’s drug-metabolism section.
**Major route (~90%):** glucuronidation and sulfation → safe urinary excretion.
**Minor route (~5–10%):** CYP2E1 oxidation → NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine), normally neutralized by glutathione (GSH) conjugation at therapeutic doses.
Mostly conjugated to inactive sulfate and glucuronide; half-life 2–3 hours, relatively unaffected by renal function.

monitoring.text: **Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.**
Patients often don’t realize a product contains acetaminophen unless they check the label — reinforce generic-name awareness.
**Acute single ingestion:** plot the acetaminophen level on the **Rumack-Matthew nomogram**; check AST/ALT.
**How to use the nomogram:** draw a level at 4 hours or later after a single acute ingestion and plot it against time since ingestion.
**Above the treatment line:** give NAC. **Below the line:** toxicity unlikely. Example: 8 h, 120 mcg/mL is above the line, so start NAC.
The illustrative treatment line runs from 150 mcg/mL at 4 h, halving every 4 h, to 4.7 mcg/mL at 24 h.
**Limits:** not valid before 4 hours, with an unknown ingestion time, or for staggered, repeated supratherapeutic, or chronic ingestion — use clinical judgment, AST/ALT, and poison control.
Start NAC without waiting if presentation is late or the level is unavailable and the ingestion is significant.
After 24 hours the nomogram is not used: 4.7 mcg/mL is only where the treatment line ends, not a safe cutoff. A detectable level or elevated AST/ALT guides NAC, per protocol or poison control.
Adults: generally no more than 4 g/day — and even 4 g is associated with more liver function test abnormalities.

pearls.text: **Antidote: N-acetylcysteine**, a glutathione precursor — it replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI.
Case: a patient on regular acetaminophen for back pain starts an OTC cold-and-flu combination. **What is the hidden danger in this combination?** Double-dosing acetaminophen.
**Antidote: NAC (N-acetylcysteine) replenishes glutathione; give early for best effect.**
Ask: “What is the danger of a cold-and-flu product on top of regular acetaminophen?” Look for unintentional double dosing from combination products.
**Other analgesics — tramadol:** weak μ-opioid agonist plus serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake inhibition; no anti-inflammatory effect; up to 300 mg/day; risks serotonin syndrome and seizures.

overview.text: Powerful anti-inflammatory effect, with real systemic risk.
**Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2.**
**Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2 over COX-1.**

prototype.text: Ibuprofen — common first-line choice for mild-moderate pain.
Diclofenac — available in oral and topical formulations.
Indomethacin — more potent, more GI/CNS adverse effects.
**Ketorolac — short-term use only, significant GI/renal risk.**

moa.text: NSAID → COX inhibition → ↓ prostaglandins → ↓ pain, inflammation, fever.
**COX-1, the “housekeeping” enzyme:** maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it causes GI and renal adverse effects.
**COX-2:** induced mainly at sites of inflammation and the primary source of inflammatory prostaglandins; selective inhibition targets inflammation with less GI toxicity.
Simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation: COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.
**Pathway:** COX converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins **and thromboxane A2 (TXA2)**. Less prostaglandin: pain, fever, and inflammation fall. Less TXA2: bleeding risk.
Every NSAID shares the COX mechanism; the side effects follow from losing protective prostaglandins (GI injury, platelet inhibition, renal effects).
**COX-1 is constitutive:** gastric mucosa (protection), platelets (TXA2, clotting), kidney (renal blood flow). **COX-2 is inducible** in inflamed tissue: pain, swelling, fever.
Nonselective NSAIDs block both isoforms, so GI injury is common. Selectivity trades anti-inflammatory benefit against GI and platelet protection.
Celecoxib selectively inhibits inducible COX-2, the main source of inflammatory prostaglandins, and largely spares COX-1 in gastric mucosa — lowering ulcer and bleeding risk.
**Celecoxib’s trade-off:** PGI2 (prostacyclin) falls without a matching drop in TXA2, which raises cardiovascular event risk; stomach and platelet protection continue.
Celecoxib still affects kidney prostaglandins, so renal risk is not eliminated.
Aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX (the effect lasts the 8–10-day life of the platelet); other nonselective NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors.
COX-2 inhibitors spare platelet thromboxane (made by COX-1) but block endothelial prostacyclin — so they are not cardioprotective.

indications.text: Oral NSAIDs for osteoarthritis — effective, but carry the systemic risks below.
Topical NSAIDs — effective local relief with much lower systemic exposure.
NSAIDs ease symptoms but, unlike DMARDs, do not alter the course of any arthritic disorder.
Used in RA, spondyloarthropathies, OA, sprains and strains, low back pain, and gout (tolmetin appears ineffective in gout).

adverse.text: **Gastrointestinal:** gastritis, peptic ulcer, GI bleeding.
**Renal:** decreased renal perfusion, fluid retention, acute kidney injury.
**Cardiovascular:** hypertension, increased risk of cardiovascular events.
**Celecoxib:** lower risk of ulcer/bleeding, but **COX-2 selectivity is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk — a key trade-off.**
Celecoxib’s renal risk is similar to nonselective NSAIDs — COX-2 selectivity does not protect the kidney.
**GI:** less prostaglandin-driven mucus and bicarbonate leaves the mucosa open to injury (ulcer, bleeding).
**Kidney:** reduced afferent arteriolar dilation lowers renal blood flow (AKI, fluid retention).
**Platelets:** reduced TXA2 impairs aggregation, increasing bleeding risk.
Beyond GI, renal, and CV: headache, tinnitus, dizziness, rare aseptic meningitis, liver test abnormalities, asthma, rashes, hyperkalemia.

contra.text: Use caution or avoid in: active GI bleeding or ulcer history; chronic kidney disease; heart failure or cardiovascular disease.
Also caution or avoid with anticoagulant therapy and in late pregnancy.
Ibuprofen is relatively contraindicated with nasal polyps, angioedema, or bronchospastic reactivity to aspirin.

interactions.text: NSAIDs + ACE inhibitors/ARBs → ↑ AKI risk; add a diuretic and it is the **“triple whammy,”** a very high-yield AKI pattern.
NSAIDs + diuretics → reduced diuretic effect, ↑ renal risk.
Ibuprofen taken with aspirin blocks aspirin’s irreversible platelet inhibition, limiting its cardioprotective effect.
Celecoxib (a CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts with warfarin and raises lithium and fluconazole levels.

pk.text: Naproxen’s longer half-life allows twice-daily dosing; diclofenac comes as oral and topical forms.
**Chemistry & pharmacokinetics:** most NSAIDs are weak acids, well absorbed, ~98% albumin-bound, metabolized by CYP3A or CYP2C, and renally excreted.

overview.text: **Osteoarthritis (OA):** primarily degenerative joint disease — cartilage breakdown with mechanical wear.
**Rheumatoid arthritis (RA):** autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease — immune-mediated joint destruction.
**OA pathophysiology:** mechanical load and wear degrade cartilage; bone remodels with osteophytes.
**RA pathophysiology:** immune activation → autoimmune synovitis forms a **pannus** that erodes cartilage and bone; **TNF-α and IL-6** drive the inflammation and joint damage.
OA treatment goal: pain control and function.
RA treatment goal: suppress disease activity, not just pain.
The hinge: OA is managed mainly with analgesics/NSAIDs, while RA requires disease-modifying therapy.
**DMARD (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug):** a drug intended to alter the course of RA, not just mask its symptoms.
**Goal of therapy:** slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation, rather than providing analgesia alone.
An NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing the disease trajectory; a DMARD is meant to change the trajectory itself.
**NSAIDs** relieve pain and swelling within days but do not alter joint damage; **DMARDs** take weeks to months to act, then slow cartilage and bone destruction.
**Timing:** judge a DMARD over months, not after the first visit — set expectations that benefit builds over months. Relief now with NSAIDs, protection later with DMARDs.
Targeted therapy: each biologic class corresponds to a different cytokine or cell type in the inflammatory cascade — the mediator list from the start of the lecture.
DMARD effects take 2 weeks to 6 months to appear. Types: conventional synthetic (cs), biologic (b), and targeted synthetic (ts, e.g., tofacitinib).
Biologics are large molecules, usually proteins made by recombinant DNA technology; JAK inhibitors are oral small-molecule targeted synthetic DMARDs.

prototype.text: **Methotrexate — the anchor drug for most RA regimens.**
Hydroxychloroquine — milder disease; relatively favorable safety profile.
Sulfasalazine — often used in combination regimens.
Leflunomide — alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated.

moa.text: **Mechanism: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing immune cell proliferation at low RA doses.** (methotrexate)
**Hydroxychloroquine** alters lysosomal and TLR signaling (less antigen signaling); **sulfasalazine** reduces cytokine and prostaglandin production.
**Leflunomide** inhibits DHODH, blocking pyrimidine synthesis (slower T-cell growth).
Conventional DMARDs act inside cells or on broad immune pathways, with a slower onset than biologics.
**Methotrexate’s folate pathway:** blocking DHFR stops dihydrofolate (DHF) → tetrahydrofolate (THF), the folate needed for purine and thymidylate (DNA) synthesis.
At low RA doses methotrexate is likely anti-inflammatory via **adenosine release**, not cytotoxicity.
TNF inhibitors block tumor necrosis factor-alpha signaling.
IL-6 inhibitors block interleukin-6 receptor signaling.
B-cell targeted therapy depletes or modulates B lymphocytes.
T-cell costimulation modulators block the second signal needed for T-cell activation.
Figure 3: abatacept acts at T-cell activation, TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab at cytokine release, rituximab at B cells — all upstream of synovial inflammation and joint destruction.
**TNF inhibitors:** antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab) and etanercept, a receptor fusion protein, neutralize soluble and membrane TNF-α, preventing TNFR activation.
**Tocilizumab** blocks both membrane and soluble IL-6 receptors.
**Abatacept (CTLA-4-Ig)** binds CD80/86 and blocks CD28 costimulation, acting early at T-cell activation.
**Rituximab (anti-CD20)** binds CD20 and depletes B cells for months.
Each biologic intercepts a different step of the immune cascade: walk it from T-cell activation to cytokines to synovial damage — abatacept acts earliest.

indications.text: **OA step 1:** acetaminophen — reasonable first-line for mild OA pain.
**OA step 2:** oral NSAIDs (effective, systemic risks) or topical NSAIDs (local relief, much lower systemic exposure).
**Intra-articular corticosteroid injections:** short-term relief for flares in a single joint.
Other approaches: activity modification, physical therapy, weight management.
**Where each OA analgesic acts:** acetaminophen centrally (brain and spinal cord COX) — little anti-inflammatory effect in the joint.
Oral or topical NSAIDs block COX in joint tissue (synovium and cartilage), lowering prostaglandins, pain, and swelling.
An intra-articular steroid calms local inflammation inside the joint for fast, short-term flare relief. Choice depends on which tissue drives the pain.
Methotrexate anchors most RA regimens; leflunomide is the alternative when it is not tolerated.
Rheumatoid arthritis: they modify the disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
TNF inhibitors are the first-line biologic; tocilizumab works as monotherapy; rituximab is used after TNF-inhibitor failure.
**Glucocorticoid drugs in rheumatic diseases:** used chronically in 30–70% of RA patients; relief is prompt and dramatic, and they slow new bone erosions.
Long-term prednisone in RA: no more than 7.5 mg daily, tapered when possible — even 2.8 mg daily for over 5 years is linked to severe infections.
Intra-articular corticosteroids often relieve painful symptoms for up to several months.
Long-term glucocorticoid harms: osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, Cushing syndrome, infections, cataract, glaucoma, gastric ulcer, depression.
Methotrexate starts at 7.5 mg weekly and rises to 15–25 mg weekly; it slows new erosions in RA.
**Combination therapy with DMARDs** is now the rule when monotherapy falls short; triple therapy (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) rivals etanercept plus methotrexate.

adverse.text: **Boxed warning — all TNF inhibitors:** possible malignancy, especially lymphoma.
**Boxed warning — all JAK inhibitors:** venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE), major adverse cardiovascular events, and cancer.
Methotrexate key adverse effects: **hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, pulmonary toxicity.**
**The major safety theme across all DMARDs: immunosuppression → increased infection risk.** This holds for conventional and biologic DMARDs alike.
**Risk:** suppressed immunity lets latent TB and opportunistic infections (TB, viral, fungal) emerge.
TNF inhibitors: watch for reactivation of latent TB. Tocilizumab can raise lipids and liver enzymes. Abatacept has a generally lower infection signal.
Methotrexate’s most common toxicities are nausea and stomatitis; dose-related liver enzyme elevations are frequent.
TNF inhibitors: TB reactivation, fungal infections, hepatitis B reactivation, new or worse heart failure, demyelinating disease, lupus-like syndrome.

contra.text: Don’t stack biologics: abatacept with a TNF inhibitor probably raises serious infections; upadacitinib with biologic DMARDs is not recommended.

interactions.text: Tocilizumab stimulates CYP450 — doses of cyclosporine or warfarin may need adjusting.
Methotrexate given with TNF inhibitors reduces anti-drug antibodies (infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab).

pk.text: **Methotrexate is dosed weekly (not daily) — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.**
**Weekly dosing only:** daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity.

monitoring.text: **Folate supplementation** is routinely co-prescribed with methotrexate to reduce toxicity.
Folic acid co-therapy reduces methotrexate’s liver, marrow, lung, and GI toxicity.
**Baseline screening:** e.g., tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C screening before starting biologics.
**Vaccination:** update vaccines, especially live vaccines, before starting therapy.
**Ongoing monitoring:** regular labs to catch cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, or infection early.
**Infection precautions:** counsel patients to report fevers or infection symptoms promptly.
**Screen first:** TB test (IGRA or TST) and hepatitis B and C serology before starting; check hepatitis B before rituximab.
**Vaccines:** update non-live vaccines before treatment.
**Monitor:** CBC and liver and kidney labs every 1–3 months; act early on fever or infection signs.
Folic acid or leucovorin reduces stomatitis, GI, and liver test problems but may cut methotrexate efficacy by 10–18%.
Hydroxychloroquine: baseline eye exam, then annual screening after 5 years (retinopathy).
Avoid live vaccines for up to 3 months after stopping abatacept; stop upadacitinib before a live attenuated vaccine.

OA and RA both affect the joint but are two very different diseases — don’t give RA patients analgesia alone.
Methotrexate’s weekly dosing is one of the highest-yield patient-safety points in all of rheumatology pharmacology.
Match each generic name to its class: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab (TNF); tocilizumab (IL-6); rituximab (B cell); abatacept (T-cell costimulation).

**Read the stem first:** it reveals the mechanism class before the drug is recalled (-mab antibody: -zumab humanized, -ximab chimeric, -umab fully human; -cept receptor fusion; -nib/-tinib kinase inhibitor; -coxib COX-2 selective; -profen, -fenac, -oxicam NSAID subclasses).
Topical diclofenac 1% gel is sold over the counter for OA and muscular pain.
**Biosimilars:** near-copies of legacy biologics with the same efficacy, toxicity, and immunogenicity at potentially lower cost.
If methotrexate alone falls short: add csDMARDs or a biologic — usually a TNF inhibitor first, then non-TNF biologics or JAK inhibitors.

hooks.text: Why can’t RA be treated like OA? RA is immune-mediated joint destruction; analgesics ease pain but leave the immune attack — and the damage — running.
Methotrexate rules = **W-F-P**: **W**eekly (never daily), **F**olate with it, **P**regnancy contraindicated.
Why screen for TB and hepatitis first? These drugs suppress the immune response that keeps latent infections in check, so a hidden infection can reactivate.
Generic-name endings: **-mab** = monoclonal antibody (adalimumab, infliximab, tocilizumab, rituximab); **-cept** = receptor-fusion protein (etanercept, abatacept).

high_yield.text: OA = degenerative → pain control; RA = autoimmune → suppress disease activity.
OA ladder: acetaminophen → oral or topical NSAIDs → intra-articular steroids for a single-joint flare.
DMARDs (conventional and biologic — methotrexate, adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, tocilizumab, rituximab, abatacept) modify RA’s disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
Methotrexate: DHFR inhibitor, **weekly**, with folate.
Methotrexate toxicity: liver, marrow, lung; teratogenic.
HCQ = milder RA; sulfasalazine = combinations; leflunomide = if MTX not tolerated.
DMARDs change disease. Methotrexate is weekly, and screen for TB and hepatitis before biologics.
TNF: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab · IL-6: tocilizumab · B cell: rituximab · T-cell costimulation: abatacept.
Shared risk: immunosuppression → infection.
Before biologics: TB + hepatitis B/C screening, update (live) vaccines.

discrepancies.text: **Methotrexate mechanism:** the slides and study guide name dihydrofolate reductase as the target (the depth slide adds a likely adenosine-mediated anti-inflammatory effect at low dose); the textbook says the DHFR effect is relatively minor at RA doses and credits AICAR transformylase, which raises extracellular AMP. Both agree the low-dose effect is anti-inflammatory rather than cytotoxic. Answer course exams with the slide/study-guide version (DHFR).

**Vaccines before DMARDs — two slides differ:** S56 says update vaccines, especially live vaccines, before starting; S57 says update non-live vaccines. Read together: bring all vaccines up to date before therapy, because live vaccines should not be given once immunosuppression has started (textbook: avoid live vaccines up to 3 months after stopping abatacept).
